prompt.context_jp: 久我山が涼香に伝える重大発表の場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「音羽＿ 厚労省を 辞めることが 決まりました」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle presents Otowa's resignation as fresh news?

feedback.correct_en: This clause 「音羽が…辞めること」 is a noun clause describing a new fact that 'has been decided.' Inside subordinate clauses that package new information for the listener, が marks the subject (音羽). は would be inappropriate inside a 「〜ことが決まる」 structure.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would push 音羽 to a topic level, but syntactically that doesn't fit inside the 〜こと nominalization leading to が決まりました. も would wrongly suggest 'Otowa too (in addition to someone).'

contrast_examples.jp: 音羽が辞めることが決まりました。
contrast_examples.en: It was decided that Otowa will resign. (new fact)

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見が世論の変化を感じ取る場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 世間の風向きが変わり、味方だった声が大幅に減少していくのを、彼＿もう肌で感じていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks Kitami as the established topic of this sentence?

feedback.correct_en: Kitami is already the known subject of this paragraph — the narration keeps him as the ongoing topic. 彼は signals topic continuity ('as for him, he was already feeling it').
feedback.incorrect_en: 彼が would newly identify him as the specific one feeling it (exhaustive), but context already established him; it would feel like introducing him afresh. 彼に doesn't fit — 感じる takes the experiencer as subject, not dative.

contrast_examples.en: He was already feeling it. (topic continues)
He was the one feeling it. (identificational)

prompt.context_jp: 朝、廊下で妹の姿を見つける場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 洗濯かごを抱えた妹の姿＿、廊下の向こうに見えた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle introduces the sister's figure as a newly perceived sight?

feedback.correct_en: 見える is intransitive ('be visible'), and the thing that becomes visible is marked with が. The sister's figure is newly brought into the narrator's field of view here, which matches the new-information が.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would treat 妹の姿 as a pre-established topic, flattening the moment-of-noticing. を would require a transitive verb like 見た.

contrast_examples.en: My sister's figure came into view.
I saw my sister's figure. (actively looked)

prompt.context_jp: 久我山が音羽の処遇について語る場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「これで お前＿厚労省に残れる」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks お前 as the topic 'as for you'?

feedback.correct_en: The speaker is informing the listener about her future outcome — 'As for you, you can stay.' This is classic topic-は, framing お前 as the person the comment is about.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make it an exhaustive 'YOU (and no one else) can stay,' which doesn't match the reassuring, informational tone. を is grammatically wrong — 残れる is intransitive potential.

contrast_examples.en: You are the one who stays. (singling out)

prompt.context_jp: 久我山がMERへの世論の反転を語る。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「世間の手のひら返し＿厳しい」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle makes 「世間の手のひら返し」 the topic being characterized?

feedback.correct_en: The speaker is characterizing a known phenomenon — the public's about-face — with a judgment ('is harsh'). は topic-marks the subject of this general evaluation.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would newly introduce the phenomenon, but in context it's already understood from the preceding lines about SNS and public opinion. に would be grammatically off here.

contrast_examples.jp: 手のひら返しは厳しいよ。
手のひら返しが始まった。

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見が妹を慰める場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「もともと 俺＿悪いから」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle best delivers Kitami's 'It's MY fault' meaning?

feedback.correct_en: Kitami is singling himself out as the one who is at fault, taking responsibility away from his sister. This is exhaustive-identification が: 'I'm the one who's to blame.'
feedback.incorrect_en: 俺は悪い would sound like a general self-assessment ('As for me, I'm bad'), losing the exculpatory nuance toward the sister. 俺も would suggest 'me too,' implying others are also at fault.

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見が妹に責任はないと伝える場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「全部 俺の責任だから 涼香＿何にも悪くない」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle sets up Ryouka in contrast to Kitami ('you — unlike me — did nothing wrong')?

feedback.correct_en: The previous clause blames 俺. Here は on 涼香 produces an implicit contrast: 'I'm to blame — you, on the other hand, aren't at all.' That's the contrastive-は use.
feedback.incorrect_en: 涼香が悪くない would single her out as 'the one who isn't bad,' which doesn't match the comforting flow. を is ungrammatical with 悪い.

contrast_examples.jp: 俺が悪い、涼香は悪くない。
contrast_examples.en: I'm the one at fault; you aren't. (contrast)

contrast_examples.jp: 涼香が悪いんじゃない。
contrast_examples.en: It's not Ryouka who's at fault. (identificational denial)

prompt.context_jp: 病院前の歩道の様子。
prompt.prompt_jp: 病院前の歩道＿、いつのまにか報道陣で埋め尽くされていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the sidewalk as the topic being described?

feedback.correct_en: The narrator is describing a scene: 'As for the sidewalk, (it) had been filled.' This is a classic topic-は set-up for a scene-setting sentence.
feedback.incorrect_en: 歩道が…埋め尽くされていた would be grammatical but would present the sidewalk as freshly identified subject; the narrator here is setting the scene by topic. を is wrong because 埋め尽くされる is a passive.

contrast_examples.jp: 歩道は人で埋まっていた。
contrast_examples.en: The sidewalk was packed with people. (scene setting)

prompt.context_jp: 副院長が懸念を伝える場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「このままでは 患者さんたち＿も迷惑がかかる」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the patients as the ones trouble is directed toward?

feedback.correct_en: 迷惑がかかる takes に to mark the person/party affected ('trouble falls on ~'). 患者さんたちにも = 'to patients as well.'
feedback.incorrect_en: で would mark a location/means, not the affected party. を is wrong because the subject of かかる is 迷惑, not 患者さん.

contrast_examples.en: It causes trouble for the family.

prompt.context_jp: 病院長の低い声が響いた瞬間。
prompt.prompt_jp: 病院長の低い声＿、部屋の空気が固まった。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the voice as the trigger/cause the room reacts to?

feedback.correct_en: 〜に固まる uses に to mark the stimulus the air 'freezes in response to.' Here the low voice is the trigger of the reaction.
feedback.incorrect_en: で would read as 'by means of' or 'at,' which doesn't match the reactive-stimulus reading. は would make the voice a topic and leave the cause-of-freezing unmarked.

contrast_examples.en: The air froze at one word. (stimulus)
He spoke in a low voice. (manner)

prompt.context_jp: 音羽が涼香を責める場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「私の手柄＿奪うなんて」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks 私の手柄 as the direct object of 奪う?

feedback.correct_en: 奪う ('to snatch/steal') is a transitive verb and its target is marked with を. Otowa is accusing Ryouka of stealing her credit.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would wrongly make 手柄 the subject. に doesn't fit the role of the stolen thing.

contrast_examples.en: Credit is stolen. (passive, が for subject)

prompt.context_jp: 音羽が涼香に自分の立場を言い放つ場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「そもそも 私＿ 医者が 危険な現場に 踏み込むべきではないと 言い続けてきました」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks 私 as the topic making this statement about her long-held view?

feedback.correct_en: Otowa is foregrounding her own stance against a backdrop of others' positions — 'As for me, I've always said…' That's topical/contrastive は on 私.
feedback.incorrect_en: 私が would make it an exhaustive identification ('I am the one who has said'), which doesn't match the general policy-statement tone. 私も would mean 'me too,' implying agreement with others.

contrast_examples.jp: 私はずっとそう言ってきた。

contrast_examples.en: I was the one who said so. (identificational)

prompt.context_jp: 椿が電話越しに脅す場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「その教室内には 私の協力者＿います」
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle introduces 'an accomplice of mine' as new information?

feedback.correct_en: いる/ある-existential clauses with newly introduced referents take が. Tsubaki is dropping new info — the existence of a mole — on his audience.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would require 協力者 to already be a known topic, but this is a reveal. を doesn't fit an existential verb.

contrast_examples.en: The accomplice has already left. (known topic)

prompt.context_jp: 久我山が世間のバッシングを描写する。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「お決まりの ＿だ」
prompt.prompt_en: Which word completes this phrase meaning 'the usual public shaming'?

feedback.correct_en: つるし上げ means 'public denunciation / scapegoating' — exactly the mob-shaming on SNS the speaker is describing.
feedback.incorrect_en: 引き上げ ('raising/withdrawal') and 立ち上げ ('launching') describe neutral or positive actions and don't fit the bullying tone.

contrast_examples.jp: ネットでのつるし上げ。

prompt.context_jp: メディアの反転を語る場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「世間の＿返しは厳しい」
prompt.prompt_en: Which word completes the idiom for 'public opinion's about-face'?

feedback.correct_en: 手のひら返し is a fixed idiom meaning 'a complete reversal of attitude' — turning the palm from facing one way to the other. Perfect for describing media/public mood flipping on MER.
feedback.incorrect_en: 手の甲 (back of the hand) and 手首 (wrist) are not idiomatic with 返し in this meaning. Only 手のひら forms this expression.

contrast_examples.jp: 手を返すように態度が変わる。
contrast_examples.en: Attitude changes as if flipping a hand.

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見が副院長に深く頭を下げる場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「ご迷惑を＿ 申し訳ありません」
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb form fits the formal apology 'for causing trouble'?

feedback.correct_en: ご迷惑をおかけして〜申し訳ありません is a fixed humble apology formula. The お+Vます stem+する pattern (おかけする) is standard business-polite self-lowering speech.
feedback.incorrect_en: かけさせて would be causative ('letting someone cause trouble') — wrong voice. かけてもらって is receiving-benefit, which inverts the responsibility.

contrast_examples.jp: ご迷惑をおかけして申し訳ありません。
contrast_examples.en: I'm sorry for the trouble I've caused. (humble)

prompt.context_jp: 久我山が涼香に取引を持ちかける場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「あなたなら 音羽を ＿ます」
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb fits 'you can save Otowa'?

feedback.correct_en: 救う ('save/rescue') is used for a person's career, life, or situation. Here it refers to saving Otowa's career — exactly the right verb.
feedback.incorrect_en: 治す is for curing illness; 直す is for fixing objects or habits. Neither fits saving a person from a political/career crisis.

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見がチームを守るために単独出動を決める。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「これ以上 皆さんやご家族に 迷惑＿ませんから」
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb form completes 'I can't cause you any more trouble'?

feedback.correct_en: 迷惑をかける is the fixed collocation. 「〜かけられません」 is the potential-negative ('cannot cause/bring myself to cause'). Kitami says he can't bring himself to burden them further.
feedback.incorrect_en: かけれ is a non-standard shortened potential form (ら抜き) and sounds off in his polite register. かからせ (causative of かかる) doesn't fit — the subject is the one doing the kakeru.

contrast_examples.jp: 迷惑をかけられません。
迷惑をかけてすみません。

prompt.context_jp: 公安の南が椿を遮る場面。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「御託はいい 要求を＿」
prompt.prompt_en: Which blunt imperative fits an officer cutting off small talk?

feedback.correct_en: 言え is the plain command form — a sharp, authoritative imperative matching a security officer's blunt tone with a terror suspect.
feedback.incorrect_en: 言って is softer and would sound polite/pleading, wrong for this confrontational moment. 言おう is volitional 'let's say,' which doesn't fit at all.

contrast_examples.jp: 要求を言ってください。

prompt.context_jp: 疑われた喜多見の静かな反論。
prompt.prompt_jp: 「俺は医者です 命を＿のが仕事です」
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb completes the MER philosophy 'to save lives'?

feedback.correct_en: 命を救う ('save a life') is the signature MER phrase repeated throughout the series, including at the chapter's opening. Kitami is reaffirming the core mission statement.
feedback.incorrect_en: 助かる is intransitive ('to be saved') and takes が, not を. 守る ('to protect') is close in meaning but the series' set phrase is specifically 命を救う.

contrast_examples.jp: 命を救うのが仕事です。
contrast_examples.en: My job is to save lives.

prompt.context_jp: 喜多見が病院長の活動停止要請に答える場面。
prompt.prompt_en: Kitami refuses the suspension order. Which line sounds most natural for his firm but respectful stance?

choices.text: それはできません。MERは解散になるかもしれませんが、それまではできるかぎりのことをしていくつもりです。
それ無理です。MERは解散になるけど、それまでできるだけやります。
それはダメです。MERは解散しますが、できる限りやるつもりだよ。

feedback.correct_en: Option A matches the actual line in the story. It balances firm refusal (それはできません) with keigo-level forward-looking resolve (〜ていくつもりです), appropriate when speaking to the hospital director.
feedback.incorrect_en: B drops into casual plain forms (無理です, やります) and sounds under-polite for addressing a superior. C mixes polite です with casual 「だよ」 which is a register clash.

prompt.context_jp: 比奈が、一人で行こうとする喜多見に抗議する。
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing captures Hina's upset-but-respectful protest to her chief most naturally?

choices.text: 勝手に決めないでください。
勝手に決めてもらっては困るんですけど。

feedback.correct_en: Option A is the actual line. 〜ないでください is firm but still polite — appropriate for Hina pushing back at her superior without crossing into rudeness.
feedback.incorrect_en: B (決めるな) is a plain-form command — too aggressive for her relationship with Kitami. C uses a passive-aggressive office tone that fits a complaint over paperwork, not an urgent emotional protest.

contrast_examples.jp: 勝手に決めないでください。
contrast_examples.en: Please don't decide on your own. (firm + polite)
Don't decide on your own! (rough command)

prompt.context_jp: 椿が電話口で挨拶する冷静な口調。
prompt.prompt_en: Which greeting most naturally captures Tsubaki's eerie-polite phone opening?

choices.text: こんにちは、喜多見先生。椿です。先生がいる病院の近くなので、必ず来てくれると思ってました。
もしもし喜多見。椿だよ。病院近いから来るよね？
やあ喜多見先生！椿でーす。病院の近くだから絶対来ると思った！

feedback.correct_en: Option A matches the actual line. The polite 先生/です form combined with calm declarative sentences creates the chilling 'courteous terrorist' register the scene requires.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is too casual/intimate (〜だよ, 喜多見 without 先生) and loses the formal menace. C is overly cheerful with elongated vowels and exclamations, which breaks the cold tone.

contrast_examples.jp: こんにちは、喜多見先生。椿です。
contrast_examples.en: Hello, Dr. Kitami. This is Tsubaki. (formal/calm)

prompt.context_jp: 久我山が妹相手に優位に立つ場面。
prompt.prompt_en: Which line best captures the smug older-brother tone in the Japanese line 「むしろ 感謝してほしいな」?

choices.text: むしろ、感謝してほしいな。
むしろ、感謝していただきたいです。

feedback.correct_en: Option A is the actual line. 〜てほしいな with the sentence-final な is a soft, almost teasing demand — exactly matching the smug-older-brother register toward his sister.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is overly polite keigo that would feel like he's addressing a superior, not his sister. C is a bare command, too harsh for the deliberately smug/breezy tone he's going for.

contrast_examples.en: I'd like you to thank me, you know. (casual/smug)

prompt.context_jp: 音羽が涼香に冷たく釘を刺す。
prompt.prompt_en: Which version most naturally renders Otowa's cold-but-polite rebuke?

choices.text: これ以上、私に迷惑をかけないでいただきたい。
これ以上、私に迷惑かけんなよ。
これ以上、迷惑かけたらダメだからね。

feedback.correct_en: Option A matches the actual line. 〜ないでいただきたい is formal/distancing polite — a classic icy-polite refusal, more cutting than casual anger would be.
feedback.incorrect_en: B is rough masculine casual (かけんなよ) — wrong gender/register for Otowa and too raw. C is scolding-friendly tone that would soften the deliberate chill of her rejection.

contrast_examples.jp: 迷惑をかけないでいただきたい。
contrast_examples.en: I would appreciate you not causing me trouble. (icy-polite)
